item.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
item.description: It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI. Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital. Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme Continue reading...

At the close of market on Thursday, Anthropic shares were trading at just over $97 with a nearly $1.3tn total market capitalization, $1.75tn fully diluted. While the final share value was higher than the IPO price of $83, it marked a dip from an early high of $111.50. The firm’s shares initially soared 34% when trading got under way on its US market debut on Thursday, valuing the company at more than $2tn. Nonetheless, Anthropic’s ranked among the biggest stock market flotations in history. item.title: From training clips to thirst traps: why athletes are turning to OnlyFans
item.description: A professional sports career does not guarantee wealth. And a growing number of athletes are turning to alternative streams of income “I’m sick and tired of it.” Bart Swings tossed his jacket behind him. It was August 2025, the Winter Olympics were less than six months away, and the Belgian Olympic champion’s injured knee was not getting better. The clip, profanity and all, later ran on the Belgian evening news along with the weather and the football. But the injury update didn’t come from an interview – it was broadcast on the speed skater’s OnlyFans channel. The subscription site, best known for porn dudes, cam girls and dubiously horny couples, has quietly assembled one of the stranger rosters in professional sport. The list, about 285 athletes deep, includes Olympic speed skaters and rowers, tennis players, surfers and golfers. And, despite its racy reputation, many of the athletes on OnlyFans are not putting out adult content. Continue reading...
